title: How does pattern matching work in C#?
description: Type, property, relational, and declaration patterns, switch expressions, and pattern-based dispatch vs the visitor problem.

data.text: **Question:** How does pattern matching work in C#?

Pattern matching tests a value against a **pattern** and, on success, **binds** extracted parts to variables — all in one expression. C# supports type patterns (`is string s`), constant and relational patterns (`is > 0`), property patterns (`is { Length: > 5 }`), positional patterns for tuples/records, and combinator patterns (`and`, `or`, `not`). `switch` statements and **switch expressions** evaluate patterns in order and require exhaustiveness for type patterns, so the compiler catches missing cases when you add a new variant.

**The pattern kinds:**
- **Type**: `if (obj is string s)` — tests type and binds `s` as string; replaces `as` + null checks
- **Constant**: `case 0:` or `is 0` — value equality
- **Relational**: `is > 0 and < 100` — `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` on IComparable values (numbers, dates, chars)
- **Property**: `is { Length: > 5, Tag: "prod" }` — recursive object-shape matching; nested: `{ Address: { City: "Pune" } }`
- **Positional**: deconstruction of tuples, records, Deconstruct methods: `is (1, not 0)`
- **Var / discard**: `is var x` always matches and binds; `_` discards
- **Combinators**: `and`, `or`, `not` compose any patterns: `is string { Length: > 3 } and not "null"`

**Switch forms:**
- `switch` **statement** with `case` arms — imperative style, fall-through forbidden (except `case` with no code? no — C# never falls through; use `or`)
- `switch` **expression** — expression returning a value: `var size = shape switch { Circle c => c.R * 2, Square s => s.Side, _ => 0 }`
- Arms run **top to bottom**; the first match wins — order arms from specific to general
- **Exhaustiveness**: for sealed hierarchies, omitting `_` and a variant is a compile error — adding `Triangle` to the hierarchy breaks every non-exhaustive switch **at compile time**, which is exactly the safety you want
- `when` clauses add guards: `case Circle c when c.R > 10:`

**Why it matters beyond syntax:**
- Replaces chains of `is`/`as`/casts and type-switch helper classes
- Makes illegal states unrepresentable in parse/validation code
- Sealed types + exhaustive switches give closed-world dispatch without virtual methods or visitors
- Property patterns work on anonymous types and records — great for filtering collections

data.title: From type checks to exhaustive matching

data.caption: Switch arms are evaluated top to bottom; the first matching arm wins, so general patterns must come last or they shadow specific ones.

data.text:
Interviewers want to assess:
- Knowing the pattern kinds and that binding happens as part of the match
- First-match-wins ordering and exhaustiveness checking
- The design angle: sealed types + exhaustive switches vs if-chains or the visitor pattern
- Awareness that property patterns recurse and compose with and/or/not

items: Placing a general type pattern before a specific one — the specific arm becomes unreachable
Forgetting exhaustiveness in switch statements with sealed hierarchies — silently falls to default
Re-binding the same variable across arms and expecting different scopes to leak
Using property patterns on nullable structs where the shape never matches
Keeping type-switch chains in libraries where a sealed record hierarchy + switch would compile-time check every variant
Overlapping `or` arms that bind variables with different names — the compiler rejects bindings that aren't definitely assigned
What does exhaustiveness mean for an abstract sealed hierarchy — and what happens when you add a new subtype?
How do property patterns interact with null?
switch expression vs switch statement — when does each read better?
How would you model a state machine so illegal transitions are unrepresentable with patterns?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Patterns test AND bind: type, constant, relational, property, positional, var/discard
Switch arms match top to bottom — specific before general
Sealed hierarchies get compile-time exhaustiveness — new variants break builds, not production
data.takeaway: Pattern matching turns runtime type juggling into declarative, compiler-checked dispatch — model your types as sealed records and let exhaustiveness do the testing for you.
